procedural_history.originating_court: Court of MM (N.I. Act), Digital Court-02/SED, Saket District Courts (Trial Court)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 13.12.2023 of the High Court of Delhi at New Delhi in CRLMC No. 970 of 2023 and CRLMA No. 3701 of 2023
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court passed an order in CRLMC No. 970 of 2023 and CRLMA No. 3701 of 2023. The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the High Court was entitled to pass any order which it thought fit in the interest of justice, stating that the High Court's discretion is confined to declining to entertain petitions and refusing to grant relief, not granting relief based solely on its own considerations.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellant-Complainant approached the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's order. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and invoked Article 142 of the Constitution to quash Complaint Case No. 5564 of 2022 and all proceedings emerging therefrom. The appellant-complainant was entitled to withdraw the deposited amount with interest.

directions: The impugned judgment to the extent it compounded the offence under Section 138, N.I. Act invoking the inherent power under Section 482, Cr.P.C. and the power under Section 147, N.I. Act stands quashed and set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in exercising its inherent power under Section 482, Cr.P.C and the power under Section 147, N.I. Act, 1881 to compound the offence u/s.138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, despite the non-consent of the complainant-appellant.

facts: The appellant filed a complaint against the respondents for an offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (dishonor of a cheque).
The respondents (the accused) appeared in court and offered to settle the matter, filing an application to compound the offence.
The Trial Court dismissed this application.
The respondents challenged this dismissal before the High Court.

The High Court, despite the complainant-appellant's refusal to consent, compounded the offence. It did so by exercising its inherent power under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) and the power to compound under Section 147 of the N.I. Act, reasoning that the complainant was 'equitably compensated'.
law: Section 147 of the N.I. Act states that every offence punishable under the Act is compoundable.
Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. grants the High Court inherent power to prevent the abuse of the process of any court or to secure the ends of justice.
The Supreme Court affirmed that the law is well-settled ('no longer res integra') on this issue.
The essential condition, or 'sine qua non', for compounding an offence under Section 138 of the N.I. Act is the consent of the complainant.
The inherent powers of the High Court under Section 482 Cr.P.C. cannot be invoked to bypass a specific statutory requirement, such as the need for the complainant's consent for compounding.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had erred by using its inherent power under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to force a compounding of the offence.

The Court clarified that the power to compound under Section 147 of the N.I. Act is not a power that a court can exercise on its own; it requires the agreement of the parties, specifically the complainant.
The High Court's justification that the complainant was 'equitably compensated' was deemed irrelevant, as it cannot substitute for the legal requirement of consent.
By ignoring the complainant's lack of consent, the High Court incorrectly applied its inherent powers and acted contrary to the established legal position.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's decision, holding that it was not justified in compounding the offence under Section 138 of the N.I. Act without the complainant's consent. The Court ruled that the consent of the complainant is mandatory for compounding such an offence, and the High Court cannot use its inherent powers under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to override this fundamental requirement. Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's judgment.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in exercising its inherent power under Section 482, Cr.P.C and the power under Section 147, N.I. Act, 1881 to compound the offence u/s.138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, despite the non-consent of the complainant-appellant.
appellant_arguments: The High Court was not justified in compounding the offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act without the consent of the complainant.
respondent_arguments: The High Court was entitled to pass any order which it thought fit in the interest of justice, including compounding the offence without the complainant's consent.

cases.case_name: State of Punjab & Ors. v. Surinder Kumar & Ors.
cases.principle: The power under Article 142 of the Constitution for doing complete justice is unique to the Supreme Court, and High Courts do not enjoy this authority. Therefore, an order passed by the Supreme Court under Article 142 cannot be a precedent for a High Court to pass a similar order.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The jurisdiction of the High Court is circumscribed by limitations declared by judicial decisions and it cannot transgress these limits on the basis of a subjective sense of justice. The High Court does not have the authority, equivalent to the Supreme Court's power under Article 142 of the Constitution, to make orders necessary for doing complete justice.
obiter: A decision is available as a precedent only if it decides a question of law.

It is desirable to assign reasons for every order or judgment, but the requirement is not imperative in the case of the Supreme Court, as one of the main reasons for disclosing grounds is to enable a higher court to examine the same.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court does not have the authority under its inherent powers in Section 482, Cr.P.C. or under Section 147, N.I. Act to compound an offence under Section 138, N.I. Act without the consent of the complainant. The power to make orders for doing "complete justice" in a case, such as quashing proceedings without the complainant's consent, is a unique authority granted to the Supreme Court under Article 142 of the Constitution, which the High Court does not enjoy.
legal_tests_applied: The inherent jurisdiction under Section 482, Cr.P.C, is to be exercised sparingly, carefully and with caution and only when such exercise is justified by the tests specifically laid down in the Section itself viz., to give effect to any order under Cr.P.C., or to prevent abuse of process of any Court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice.

A distinction must be made between the circumscribed jurisdiction of the High Court and the power of the Supreme Court under Article 142 of the Constitution to make such orders as may be necessary “for doing complete justice in any case or matter pending before it”, which authority the High Court does not enjoy.
why_appellant_lost: While the appellant won on the question of law that the High Court's order was incorrect, they ultimately lost the ability to continue the prosecution because the Supreme Court itself decided to quash the complaint. The Supreme Court exercised its unique power under Article 142 of the Constitution, citing the peculiar facts of the case: the deposit of the cheque amount by the respondent, the respondent's expressed readiness to pay and settle the matter, and the conclusion that there was no point in restoring the proceedings to the trial Court.
why_respondent_won: While the respondent lost the legal argument that the High Court was justified in its order, they ultimately won because the criminal proceedings against them were quashed. The Supreme Court, after setting aside the High Court's judgment, invoked its own special powers under Article 142 to quash the complaint, thereby granting the respondent the final relief they sought. This was done because the respondent had deposited the amount and shown a readiness to settle, making further proceedings fruitless.
policy_considerations: The jurisdiction of the High Court, while dealing with a writ petition, is circumscribed by the limitations discussed and declared by the judicial decisions, and it cannot transgress the limits on the basis of whims or subjective sense of justice varying from Judge to Judge.
Once an accused accepts his liability to pay the cheque amount, there will be no fruitful purpose in keeping the complaint alive.

In the interest of justice and to prevent the abuse of the process of law, when a complainant has been reasonably compensated, the accused can be discharged/acquitted even without the complainant's consent, but this power to do 'complete justice' is vested with the Supreme Court under Article 142.
